pillar_reactions.evidence: Engaged on mechanics rather than reacting: 'Is with the three to four sessions, that's like, that's all you need to do the whole week? Or is there cardio? Is there other things besides the mobility end of it?' and later 'How many people is he training at one time?' Understood and accepted the model but wanted the operating detail before agreeing.

Low-friction — he was already tracking loosely and agreed to the eating-window change without pushback: 'Yeah, whatever. Again, I'm there for whatever makes sense, right? So the end goal, if that's what I need to do, honestly, that makes my life easier.'

Asked practical and privacy questions rather than engaging with the accountability premise: 'the videos and everything is just private, right? Because I'm a super private.' and 'am I, through this process, am I also speaking to you as well too?' He never contested the pillar but never tied it to his own goal either.

anchors.raw: Because I've seen online that people are saying it's different than what you're mentioning... I don't know. They were saying it was like almost half of that.
anchors.note: The most commercially significant anchor in the batch, because it came from the company's own footprint rather than a competitor. A prospect arrived having read that the price was roughly $3,000, and the rep had no reconciliation available. The $4,000 three-month tier was invented in the next sentence to explain it away. Whatever is circulating online is setting a price expectation the sales floor cannot answer.

anchors.raw: I was thinking of getting some, you know, power rack and dumbbells and everything. I don't know if that's the right thing for me. I've been questioning that for a while, and it's a big investment, which, you know, I can afford.
anchors.note: Unlike the Erim call the same week, this prospect had already talked himself out of the equipment route — 'I'm not sure if I can sustain it for, you know, two years, three years, because I've been there' — so the alternative was neutralised before price was named. It also establishes affordability in his own words.

anchors.raw: Trevor's coached over 1200 people. If we wouldn't know what we were doing, then we probably also wouldn't be sitting here because he has 1.2 million followers.
anchors.note: The only trust asset the rep has and he used it twice, both times in place of answering a specific request. The prospect's response was to keep asking for something verifiable — 'is there another like website or something where you see all of the other transformations' — right up to the end of the call.

unmet_demand.want: Downside protection — a refund, an exit point or any structure that reduces the risk of paying $6,000 upfront to someone he has never met
unmet_demand.why_unmet: No refund policy, trial or milestone exists, and the rep declined the request as a matter of principle rather than policy: 'Not necessarily. The reason I'm saying that is then they're looking into problems.'

unmet_demand.want: A public, browsable record of client transformations outside the Instagram feed
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Asked at the very end of the call and answered with 'On Instagram you can see a whole bunch. I don't think there's a specific website.' There is no owned proof asset to point a prospect at.

unmet_demand.want: A consistent, verifiable price he could reconcile with what he had read online
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The rep did not know the source of the lower figure and constructed a tier to account for it rather than correcting it. The prospect explicitly said he was not playing games — 'I'm just trying to understand' — and left with a structure invented in the moment.
